questions.prompt: Which of these is a buying signal?

options.text: “How would that work with our memberships?”

questions.reveal: A “how” question means they’re picturing using it.

questions.prompt: “How do other studios like ours handle that?” What does it tell you?

options.text: They want proof it works for businesses like theirs

questions.reveal: Answer briefly with an example, then ask.

questions.prompt: What do you do after a buying signal?
questions.reveal: A signal is a door, not a cue to keep talking.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a buying signal?

options.text: “My manager would want to see this.”

questions.reveal: Polite filler. Ask a question to find out where they are.

questions.prompt: “Yeah, that’s exactly our problem.” What now?

options.text: Play it back and ask for the meeting

questions.reveal: You’ve connected value. Go.

questions.prompt: Why are more meetings lost by talking past the moment than by asking too early?

options.text: Their attention moves on while you keep pitching
Managers track how long calls run

questions.reveal: The moment there’s a reason to meet, go.

questions.prompt: What is a trial close?

options.text: A small yes that checks they’re with you before you ask

questions.reveal: It tests the water without asking for the meeting yet.

questions.prompt: What’s the best trial close after they name a pain?

options.text: “Would it help to see how that works with your schedule?”

questions.reveal: A yes here makes the ask easy.

questions.prompt: They say yes to your trial close. What next?
questions.reveal: Don’t make them say yes twice.

questions.prompt: When have you earned the ask?

options.text: After ten minutes on the phone
They’ve named something that isn’t working and engaged with a question

questions.reveal: That’s the bar.

questions.prompt: What does the prospect NOT need before you ask?

options.text: To know the price or agree we’re better

questions.reveal: None of that is your job on this call.

questions.prompt: Mid-pitch, the owner says “Okay, I’d be open to seeing it.” What now?

options.text: Stop selling and book the time

questions.reveal: Talking past yes costs you the meeting.

questions.prompt: Which ask is direct and specific?

options.text: “Do you maybe want to set some time aside?”
“Let’s do Thursday at 10. Does that work?”

questions.reveal: Confident, assumptive, specific.

questions.prompt: What’s the right order for a firm ask?

options.text: Playback of their pain, the reason to meet, a specific time, who should be there

questions.reveal: Their words first, then make it easy to say yes.

questions.prompt: Why name one specific time?

options.text: It’s easier to say yes to than choosing from options

questions.reveal: Don’t make them choose from a thousand options.

questions.prompt: “It’s only 30 minutes, I promise.” What’s wrong with it?

options.text: It apologizes for the meeting; say it like the next logical step

questions.reveal: The meeting isn’t a favor you’re asking for.

questions.prompt: Which playback best opens the ask?

options.text: “So it’s the manual reporting across three locations.”

questions.reveal: Their pain, their words.

questions.prompt: She says Thursday doesn’t work. Best move?

options.text: Offer another specific time, still within the next few days

questions.reveal: Stay specific and stay close.

questions.prompt: “Sure, send me something.” Best response?

options.text: “Happy to. So it’s not just another email, let’s put 20 minutes on the calendar. Tomorrow at 2?”

questions.reveal: Agree, then turn it into a time.

questions.prompt: “Let me check with my business partner.” Best response?

options.text: Wait for her to call back
“Makes sense. Let’s find a time that works for both of you. Is she usually free mornings?”

questions.reveal: Bring the partner in instead of waiting on them.

questions.prompt: “Call me next week.” Best response?

options.text: “Will do. Let’s lock in the time now so it doesn’t slip. Tuesday at 11?”

questions.reveal: A callback with no time usually doesn’t happen.

questions.prompt: “I’ll look at my calendar and get back to you.” Best response?

options.text: “Easy. Have you got it open now? I’ll hold Wednesday at 3.”

questions.reveal: Do it together while you have them.

questions.prompt: What’s the principle for stalls at the ask?

options.text: Agree with the stall, then turn it into a specific time

questions.reveal: Same posture as objection handling, aimed at a time.

questions.prompt: “Honestly, I’d only be saying yes to get off the phone.” What do you do?

options.text: Don’t book: respect it, or go back to discovery for a real reason, and log it honestly

questions.reveal: A forced meeting becomes a no-show.

questions.prompt: What does an agenda do?

options.text: Makes the meeting feel worth keeping and tells the AE what matters

questions.reveal: It’s the reason to show up.

questions.prompt: Which agenda is strongest?

options.text: “You said reporting eats your Monday. The AE will walk you through how that looks in Momence. About 30 minutes.”

questions.reveal: Their reason, what the AE will show, how long.

questions.prompt: A studio manager says the owner usually weighs in on software. Best move?

options.text: Ask whether the owner should join, and pick a time that works for both

questions.reveal: The manager can book. Inviting the owner means the meeting doesn’t have to happen twice.

questions.prompt: Why ask who else should be there?

options.text: So the decision-maker hears it firsthand and the meeting doesn’t have to happen twice

questions.reveal: It protects the meeting.

questions.prompt: What goes first in the agenda?
questions.reveal: Start with why they said yes.

questions.prompt: She agrees to Thursday at 10 and the agenda. What’s next?

options.text: Send the invite while you’re still on the phone and ask her to accept it

questions.reveal: Then everything you learned for Yes to Meeting Held takes over.
